claims.text: Nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts can catalyze ethanol oxidation.
Standard rapid quenching produces PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts with high atomic disorder.
Standard rapid quenching produces PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts with significant lattice strain.
Standard rapid quenching produces PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts with some surface segregation.
Elevated-temperature annealing with controlled cooling promotes atomic ordering in PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts.
Elevated-temperature annealing with controlled cooling increases compositional homogeneity in PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts.
Increased atomic ordering and homogenization reduce lattice strain.
Increased atomic ordering and homogenization reduce surface segregation.
Lattice strain, defect density, and compositional heterogeneity are equivalent descriptions of the proposed structural mediator.
Defect sites accelerate catalyst deactivation and poisoning during ethanol oxidation.
Reducing lattice strain and local elemental segregation minimizes the formation of deactivation-promoting defect sites.
Minimizing defect sites helps preserve active sites and thereby improves catalyst durability.
Annealed PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts will degrade more slowly than rapidly quenched catalysts during ethanol oxidation.
Improved durability will manifest as more stable current retention and a lower deactivation rate.
The proposed relationship should hold in acidic electrolyte at temperatures of approximately 70–100 degrees Celsius under typical operating potentials.
Very high temperatures or non-acidic environments may cause behavior that deviates from the durability prediction.
XRD can be used to evaluate lattice strain and crystallinity in the compared catalysts.
TEM can be used to assess atomic ordering and defect density in the compared catalysts.
